name: Essential amino acids (EAAs)

lead: EAA powder is used to support muscle building and to help keep muscle while dieting. It supplies the nine amino acids humans must get from food: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine.

Amino acids, particularly leucine, signal through mTOR to switch on muscle protein synthesis, and much of the research centers on leucine content in older adults. Studies on healthy young lifters comparing EAA powders with whole protein for visible physique outcomes are limited.

paras: Lifters mix the free-form powder into water and sip it around training or during a cut, as an alternative to protein shakes. It is often flavored and treated as an intra-workout drink.

Human safety data at typical supplement doses were not found in the sources reviewed; mouse work on branched-chain amino acids raises open metabolic questions. People with specific amino acid metabolism disorders avoid supplements.

Essential amino acids: nutrition and environmental footprint

chain: Muscle kept or built while dieting
angle.text: Fitness users take EAA powder as an alternative to protein powder: it supplies the nine essential aminos, drives muscle protein synthesis and helps muscle be kept or built while cutting. How it compares with ordinary protein for appearance has not been studied.

lead: Essential amino acids (EAAs) are nine amino acids that humans cannot synthesise fast enough to meet needs and must obtain from food: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine [1]. EAA supplements sell these as a free-form powder, positioned in fitness communities as an alternative or add-on to protein powder.

People use them to support the chain that builds a better physique: amino acids stimulate muscle protein synthesis, which supports recovery and growth from training, which over time means more muscle. Lifters on T Nation training logs describe sipping EAAs with carbohydrates during long sessions and while dieting, when they want amino acids without a full meal [2][3][4].

Research shows EAAs stimulate muscle protein synthesis, and much of this work centres on leucine content in older adults [5][6]. Trials of EAA-containing supplements in sarcopenic older adults and in people in energy deficit exist [7][8][9]; studies of EAA powders in healthy young lifters measuring visible physique outcomes are limited.
infobox: Review cites 1.4-2 g/kg/day for intense trainers [13]

paras: In bodybuilding and strength forums, EAAs are taken to support muscle gain and to hold on to muscle while cutting. T Nation log posters describe adding EAAs and carbohydrates to an intra-workout drink for long sessions, or using about 10 g of EAAs alongside creatine and a carbohydrate source [2][4]. One lifter describes taking carbohydrate plus EAAs during training after picking up the idea from a coach's tips and reports steadier hunger and energy [3]. Another mixes them into a drink as a way to add protein [10].

Outside the gym, EAA mixtures are studied in sarcopenia, cancer-related wasting and surgery recovery. A review of nutrition around orthopaedic surgery discusses amino acid and protein support for preserving muscle, strength and function [11]. A systematic review of sarcopenia interventions in older adults examined nutrition and exercise approaches [12].

Early 20th-century work showed rats failed on the maize protein zein but recovered with milk casein; William Cumming Rose then identified the essential amino acids, finding ten for rats and eight for adult humans, with histidine later shown essential for adults [1]. Rose used purified amino acid diets in graduate students and measured nitrogen balance [1].

Requirements are expressed per kilogram of body mass per day and have been revised over the past two decades; adult leucine figures are around 39 (WHO) to 42 (US) mg/kg/day [1]. Protein quality depends on essential amino acid balance, and the limiting amino acid determines how well a meal meets needs [1]. Animal proteins are described as complete sources of all essential amino acids, and plant proteins as often lacking some [13]. Egg protein is noted as highly digestible and an excellent source of essential amino acids [14].

sections.h: The nine essential and conditionally essential amino acids
paras: The nine essential amino acids are histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine.[1] Six more (arginine, cysteine, glycine, glutamine, proline and tyrosine) are classed as conditionally essential, meaning the body normally makes them but production can fall short under stresses such as prematurity or severe catabolic illness; alanine, aspartic acid, asparagine, glutamic acid and serine are non-essential.[1]

The limiting amino acid, the one furthest below its requirement, sets the nutritional value of a food, and several scoring systems (biological value, net protein utilisation, protein efficiency ratio and PDCAAS) rank protein quality.[1] Requirements are higher in children, 10 to 20 percent higher from age three and up to 150 percent higher in the first year of life, and the WHO and the US National Academy of Medicine publish different figures.[1]

Resistance-trained people encounter EAAs as a free-form alternative to whey or other protein powders. Because free amino acids need no digestion of intact protein, they are marketed as fast-absorbing; users in training logs describe sipping them through long sessions or during a calorie deficit.[2][3][4] The appearance rationale is the standard one in muscle building: keeping muscle protein synthesis stimulated supports recovery, which supports continued training and, over months, muscle size and retention while dieting.[5][13]

Mixed-protein products and whole foods supply the same essential amino acids, and the review of protein for exercise and recovery states that intense trainers need 1.4 to 2 g/kg per day, which can usually be reached from food.[13] Research on free-form EAAs has centred on older adults and clinical groups, where leucine proportion and anabolic signalling were the questions examined.[5][15][16]

Amino acids are required for activation of mTOR, a kinase that regulates protein translation, cell growth and autophagy. A 2009 Cell paper found that uptake of glutamine and its rapid efflux in the presence of essential amino acids is the rate-limiting step in activating mTOR [6]. Branched-chain amino acids, the subset of leucine, isoleucine and valine, have been studied for post-exercise soreness and mTOR activation, while an animal literature raises metabolic concerns [17].

A 2003 study in healthy elderly adults reported that essential amino acids are primarily responsible for the amino acid stimulation of muscle protein anabolism [15]. Research on ageing muscle describes anabolic signalling deficits that blunt the response to amino acids [16].

A controlled trial in young and elderly volunteers compared 6.7 g of EAAs modelled on whey (26% leucine) with a leucine-enriched mix (41% leucine); the study measured muscle protein metabolism and concluded a high proportion of leucine was required for optimal stimulation in the elderly [5].

A randomised trial in sarcopenic elderly combined whey protein (22 g), essential amino acids (10.9 g, including 4 g leucine) and vitamin D with controlled physical activity, and reported increases in fat-free mass, strength and function [9]. Because the supplement was a combination, the contribution of the EAAs alone is not separated.

A review of protein for exercise and recovery states that intense trainers require more protein than sedentary people (1.4-2 g/kg/day), that this can usually be reached through diet, and that protein or amino acids before, during or after exercise can enhance recovery and growth and maintenance of lean mass [13].

Deficiency of any one essential amino acid limits protein synthesis whatever the others supply [1]. Human safety data at typical supplement doses are limited in the material reviewed. BCAA research in mice has raised questions about metabolic and neurological effects that are not established in humans [17]. In liver disease, a review describes the efficacy of BCAA supplementation as uncertain and controversial because studies vary [18].

Registered trials examine EAA-enriched whey with carbohydrate during energy deficit in 17 participants [7], EAAs and protein kinetics during caloric deprivation in 20 [8], and supplementation in sarcopenic obesity in 80 [19]. Further registered studies cover military winter training with protein- and energy-enhanced foods (68 participants) [20], EAA intake in weight-losing lung cancer patients (41) [21] and nutritive blood flow and anabolic resistance in older adults (40) [22]. These populations are people in energy deficit or with muscle loss. No study reviewed tests EAA powders for appearance outcomes in healthy lifters.

lore.intro: On T Nation, EAAs appear mostly in training logs as an intra-workout or cutting-phase addition, usually mentioned in passing next to carbohydrates, creatine and whey [2][3][4].
